{"url": "https://export.arxiv.org/api/query?search_query=all%3Acomputational+models+of+accountability+and+consequence+tracking+in+autonomous+systems&max_results=4", "scope": "paper abstracts; preprints, peer-review status not verified", "excerpt": "title: Semi-Supervised Visual Tracking of Marine Animals using Autonomous Underwater Vehicles
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2302.07344v1
published: 2023-02-14T21:08:52Z
summary: In-situ visual observations of marine organisms is crucial to developing behavioural understandings and their relations to their surrounding ecosystem. Typically, these observations are collected via divers, tags, and remotely-operated or human-piloted vehicles. Recently, however, autonomous underwater vehicles equipped with cameras and embedded computers with GPU capabilities are being developed for a variety of applications, and in particular, can be used to supplement these existing data collection mechanisms where human operation or tags are more difficult. Existing approaches have focused on using fully-supervised tracking methods, but labelled data for many underwater species are severely lacking. Semi-supervised trackers may offer alternative tracking solutions because they require less data than fully-supervised counterparts. However, because there are not existing realistic underwater tracking datasets, the performance of semi-supervised tracking algorithms in the marine domain is not well understood. To better evaluate their performance and utility, in this paper we provide (1) a novel dataset specific to marine animals located at http://warp.whoi.edu/vmat/, (2) an evaluation of state-of-the-art semi-supervised algorithms in the context of underwater animal tracking, and (3) an evaluation of real-world performance through demonstrations using a semi-supervised algorithm on-board an autonomous underwater vehicle to track marine animals in the wild.

As AI-mediated decisions spread across organizations, accountability is often addressed through legal liability, ethics guidelines, or ad hoc managerial responses. This paper argues that such approaches fail to capture a deeper structural problem: accountability collapses when decision authority, exception response, and responsibility are not coherently aligned. We conceptualize accountability as a protocol rather than a role or rule, and examine how responsibility becomes displaced onto individuals or functions when decision boundaries are undefined. The paper demonstrates why existing organizational roles cannot absorb this burden and why accountability must be designed as part of decision infrastructure. This paper does not advocate technological restraint, but seeks to clarify the structural conditions under which accountability protocols become necessary.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6238138\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.4018/979-8-2600-2870-4.ch007\", \"title\": [\"Determining Responsibility for Artificial Intelligence-Based Security Decision Making\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The chapter discusses the determination of who is responsible when artificial intelligence is used for security decision making within complex organizational environments. {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=mechanisms+of+consequence-sensitive+agency+and+ethical+accountability+in+reinforcement+learning+agents&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.35802/227608\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.35802/227608\"}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6793998\", \"title\": [\"UG-CPPO: Uncertainty-Gated LLM Infusion for Risk-Sensitive Reinforcement Learning Trading Agents\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Recent work on hybrid Reinforcement Learning-Large Language Model (RL-LLM) trading agents, notably FinRL-DeepSeek [Benhenda, 2025], has revealed a counterintuitive empirical finding: increasing LLM signal infusion strength systematically degrades agent performance, even at perturbation magnitudes as small as 0.1%. We hypothesize that a key factor in this degradation is the absence of epistemic uncertainty estimation on LLM outputs: the agent has no mechanism to distinguish a high-confidence financial signal from an unreliable hallucination. Drawing inspiration from Monte Carlo Dropout techniques in medical imaging uncertainty quantification [Gal and Ghahramani, 2016], we propose UG-CPPO (Uncertainty-Gated CVaR-PPO), a novel architecture that dynamically gates LLM signal infusion based on prompt-ensemble-derived uncertainty. We query the LLM with N =5 semantically diverse prompts per news article and compute the standard deviation σ across responses; when σ exceeds a threshold τ , the gate closes and the signal is suppressed. We apply this gating mechanism to both the action modifier S f (PPO action perturbation) and the risk modifier R f (CVaR penalty). We evaluate the framework on the FNSPID dataset [Dong et al., 2024] with 28,502 (ticker, date) signals computed via OpenAI gpt-4o-mini, using 10seed evaluation on Nasdaq trading 2019-2023. The gating mechanism achieves the predicted activation rate (34.2% ± 0%, exactly within target [30-40%]) and we demonstrate that LLM uncertainty σ is structurally higher in bear markets (2022: 0.614) than in bull periods (2019: 0.525). However, at our computeconstrained scale (500,000 training steps, 10 stocks), UG-CPPO does not show statistically significant performance improvement over baselines on aggregate metrics (Wilcoxon p &gt; 0.05): cumulative return 36.0% ± 3…
